DIFFERENTIAL RESPONSES TO HEAT STRESS IN NORMAL AND DWARF CHICKENS:

IMPLICATIONS FOR MEAT QUALITY AND IMMUNE FUNCTION

Ali Hassan Nawaz1,3, Fujian Wang1, Zhenhai Jiao1, Weilu Zhang1, Jiahui Zheng1, Junli Sun2, Zijing Zhu1, Shudai Lin1, Li Zhang1, Junyuan Lin1♦

1College of Coastal Agricultural Sciences, Guangdong Ocean University, 524088, Zhanjiang, Guangdong, PR China 2Animal Husbandry Research Institute of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, 530214, Nanning, Guangxi, PR China

3College of Animal Science and Technology, Nanjing Agricultural University, Nanjing 210095, PR China

♦Corresponding author: jylin1016@gdou.edu.cn

Abstract This study investigated the impact of heat stress (HS) on meat quality, antioxidant ability, and immunity in normal and dwarf-size chick­ ens. A total of 144 chickens, with 72 from the normal yellow chicken (NYC) strain and 72 from the dwarf yellow chicken (DYC) strain, were equally divided into groups exposed to heat stress (35±1°C for 8 hours daily) and those kept at 28±1°C as the control group. After seven days of treatment, meat color parameters, including lightness (L*-value), redness (a*-value), and yellowness (b*-value), were as­ sessed. Histopathological examination was conducted on spleen tissues to assess structural changes. Gene expression analysis determined the expression levels of interleukin-4 (IL-4), IL-6, and liver catalase (CAT) related to immune response and antioxidant capacity. HS sig­ nificantly affected meat color parameters, with an increase in lightness (L*-value) (P<0.01) and a decrease in redness (a*-value) (P<0.01) observed in breast and thigh muscles. Furthermore, HS led to increased drip loss (P<0.05), cooking loss (P<0.05), and shear force (P<0.01) in breast muscles. Histopathological examination of spleen tissues revealed varying degrees of lymphoid depletion, necrosis, fibrosis, and inflammatory cell infiltration in response to HS. Gene expression analysis showed that HS upregulated the expression of interleukin-4 (IL-4) and IL-6 in the spleen of NYC (P<0.05) but not in DYC. Additionally, HS reduced the expression of liver catalase (CAT) in NYC (P<0.05) but had no significant effect on DYC. These findings indicate that HS adversely affects meat quality, immune response, and an­ tioxidant capacity in broilers, with normal-sized chickens being more susceptible to these effects compared to dwarf chickens. The results provide valuable insights into the differential responses of chicken strains to HS and underscore the importance of considering genetic factors in mitigating the negative impacts of heat stress on poultry production.

Key words: chicken, dwarf, meat quality, heat stress, gene expression

The production of high-quality animal protein for human consumption and the economy relies heavily on the poultry industry. However, several factors, such as environmental stress, impact the efficiency of poultry production (Ahmed-Farid et al., 2021; Pritchett et al., 2023). The imminent threat posed by global warming to the poultry industry in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide is serious. High ambient temperatures are a well-known stressor that can lead to various health and productivity problems in broiler birds (Fernandes et al., 2023; Nawaz et al., 2021; Wasti et al., 2021 a). Commer­ cial birds can only perform well in temperate climates due to their unique genotype; hence, raising them in tropical areas with hot climates frequently results in sig­ nificant economic losses (Cartoni Mancinelli et al., 2023; Wasti et al., 2020). Some studies have reported that the issue of heat stress can be addressed by introducing local genotypes such as dwarfism, which could help birds to have better thermoregulation (Yunis and Cahaner, 1999). Fast-growing commercial breeds can accelerate their growth rate due to higher metabolic activity, ultimately producing more metabolic heat. As a result, commercial

breeds perform dramatically worse in warmer situations as they strive to minimize metabolic heat production by consuming less feed (Gonzalez-Rivas et al., 2020; Nawaz et al., 2021; Wasti et al., 2021 b). Interestingly, some local chicken breeds with lower growth rates, smaller body sizes, low egg production, and low feather mass on their skin had better thermoregulation (Boonkum et al., 2021; Loengbudnark et al., 2023). For example, dwarf chicken has been reported to perform better under heat stress (HS) due to their lower body weight and less pro­ duction of metabolic heat (Nawaz et al., 2023; Sharifi et al., 2010). The dwarf trait in chickens is characterized by 1.7 kb deletion in the growth hormone receptor gene that reduces the body size of the chicken (Ouyang et al., 2012).

Depending on its degree and duration, heat stress can have a serious impact on birds’ health and ability to per­ form. It may have a negative impact on the health of poul­ try by disrupting normal metabolism, which in turn causes poor meat quality, oxidative stress, immunological sup­ pression, and mortality in chickens (Cartoni Mancinelli et al., 2023). Numerous findings have indicated that high am­

bient temperature influences the expression level of differ­ ent immune marker genes, such as interleukins (ILs) and Toll-like receptors in the chicken spleen (He et al., 2019; Varasteh et al., 2015). Cytokines, crucial immune genes that act as endogenous signaling molecules protecting cells during thermal stress. ILs are naturally occurring proteins regulating immune response under stress conditions. Proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, and IL-18 could regulate the inflammatory response, especially dur­ ing thermal stress (Helwig and Leon, 2011). Likewise, a few studies have confirmed that the expression level of proinflammatory genes is enhanced under heat stress through the activation of lymphocytes and macrophage prolifera­ tion (He et al., 2019; Varasteh et al., 2015). Therefore, in­ vestigating the impact of heat stress on immune function and exploring potential differences between chicken strains can contribute to the development of heat stress resilience strategies and effective disease management approach­ es.

Furthermore, heat stress triggers the production of reactive species, disrupting the balance between total antioxidant capacity and reactive species (Belhadj Sli­ men et al., 2014; Mujahid et al., 2007). Several radi­ cals and metabolic elements, including reactive oxygen/ nitrogen/chlorine species are potentially toxic (Belhadj Slimen et al., 2014; Del Vesco and Gasparino, 2013). These highly reactive oxidative substances can alter the structure of several biologically cellular macro­ molecules, such as proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) (He et al., 2018). Previous gene ex­ pression studies revealed that oxidative stress could be triggered by the NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4) gene (Goel et al., 2021). It is essential to mention that superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione peroxi­ dase are anti-oxidative enzymes and act as the first line of defense to counter oxidative stress. Various antioxidant enzymes such as SOD and CAT control the excessive production of oxidative species. Because SOD degrades free radicals to hydrogen peroxide, while CAT breaks down hydrogen peroxide to water and molecular oxygen (Azad et al., 2010; Kikusato and Toyomizu, 2013). These findings higlight the importance of studying antioxidant enzyme’s gene expression profiles for accurate evalua­ tion of oxidative stress under heat stress conditions.

The present study aimed to investigate the influence of heat stress on meat quality, antioxidant ability, and immune response in two different chicken strains: nor­ mal yellow chicken (NYC) and dwarf yellow chicken (DYC). NYC represents the conventional broiler breed, while DYC is a smaller-sized breed with a specific ge­ netic mutation in the growth hormone receptor gene (1.7 kb deletion mutation in cGHR) (Ouyang et al., 2012). By comparing these two strains under heat stress conditions, we sought to elucidate potential advantages or differ­ ences in their physiological and biochemical responses to heat stress. Understanding the differential responses of these strains to heat stress can contribute to the devel­ opment of strategies to enhance heat stress resilience in

broiler chickens, improve meat quality, and ensure sus­ tainable poultry production under harsh environmental conditions.

Material and methods

Animal ethics Experimental birds Both NYC and DYC are local chicken strains mainly found in China. The DYC, characterized by low body weight and short shank length, was obtained from the Ani­ mal Husbandry Research Institute of Guangxi Zhuang Au­ tonomous Region. In DYC, 1.7 kb deleted mutation in the growth hormone receptor gene is responsible for dwarfism (Ouyang et al., 2012), while the NYC had no mutation in this gene and we have confirmed this before starting heat stress experiment. The NYC with normal size was acquired from Wannong Company in Guangdong province. The chickens were reared for 12 weeks under normal environ­ ment with provision of standard feed. The feed composition and nutritive value of feed has been provided in Table 1.

Heat stress experiment HS experiment was conducted in Zhanjiang (coastal area of South China) with lengthy summer season char­ acterized by warm and humid climate. All chickens were raised to 12 weeks of age under normal environmental conditions depending on the age of birds. A total of 144 chickens were utilized in this experiment, with 72 chickens

from each strain divided equally between the heat stress (HS) and control (CN) groups. At the age of 12 weeks, 72 chickens from each strain were divided into two groups, HS (heat stress) group and CN (control) group. Each group was further divided into 6 replicates and every replicate had 6 chickens. Chickens were kept at 28±1°C ambient temperature in the CN group, while chickens were reared at 35±1°C for 8 hours daily for 7 days in the HS group, with the relative humidity at 60±5% in both groups.

Sample collection After 7 days, all chickens were weighed to compare the growth rate between the CN and the HS groups. Then they were randomly selected for collection of the tissue sam­ ples, including spleen, liver, breast muscle (the left side portions of the pectoralis major) and thigh muscle tissues.

Meat quality tests The pH values of the thigh muscle and breast muscle were determined (1 h after slaughter) with a pH meter, and the av­ erage was calculated from three readings taken at different locations. Meat color, such as lightness (L*), redness (a*), and yellowness (b*) of both breast muscle and thigh muscle samples, was determined by a colorimeter (Opto-Lab/Star Matthaus, Germany). One cm thick and 0.5 cm long strips of meat (without tendons, fascia, or fat) were used to measure the muscle shear force with a C-LM2 type muscle tender­ ness meter. Each sample was measured three times.

The water loss rate was determined through the pressurized gravimetric method. The breast and thigh muscle samples were cut into thin slices and accurately weighed for W1 (accurate up to 0.0001). After that, the sample was placed between the upper and lower layers of filter paper, fixed with a rigid plastic plate, and given a pressure of 343 N (or 35 kg). After 5 min, the pressure was removed, the sample weighed again for W2, and the water loss rate calculated by using the following formula:

Water loss rate (%) = (W1-W2)/W1×100%.

For cooking loss, weighed 2 g of sample W1 from both breast and thigh muscle tissues within 45 min af­ ter slaughter. The weighed samples were placed into the cooking pot, steamed for 0.5 h at 80°C, and then placed in a cool place for 2 h to weigh W2 and the weight differ­ ence for cooking loss was calculated.

Cooking loss (%) = (W2-W1)/W1×100%.

To measure the drip loss of each sample, about 10 g of meat sample  W1 was taken, and the weighed meat was hooked with a wire vertically downward (the direction of the muscle fibers should be consistent with the direction of grav­ ity) by suspending in an inflatable plastic bag. The bag was tied tightly to avoid contact between the meat sample and the bag wall. The sample was placed in the refrigerator for 24 h at 4°C. After 24 h, the sample was removed from the refrigera­ tor, weighed for W2, and the drip loss was calculated.

Drip loss (%) = (W1-W2)/W1×100%.

Histopathological examination The spleen and liver tissue samples were employed for histopathological examination. For histopathological assessment, tissues were cut into 4 μm thickness slices and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). In this study, an Olympus light microscope was used to examine the histological slides, while digital visuals of respective slides were procured through a Nikon DS-U3 camera linked to Nikon Eclipse CI upright optical microscope.

RNA extraction and cDNA synthesis RNA isolation from various tissues, including the liver, spleen, and breast muscles were conducted through HiPure Universal RNA kits with Trizol reagent (Magen Biotech Co. Ltd., Guangzhou, China) according to the guidelines provided by manufacturer. After RNA isola­ tion, its integrity and purity were confirmed through Na­ nodrop. Afterwards, total RNA was transcribed into the cDNA using the PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit (TaKaRa, Kyoto, Japan) following the instructions and diluted up to 4 times by adding RNase-free water. Then the cDNA was stored in refrigerator at −20°C for further use.

Real-time quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR) Real-time quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed by the Applied Biosystems StepOne PlusTM Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) using TransStart® Green qPCR SuperMix (Transgen Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). Specific primers for target genes (IL-4, IL-6, IL-10, IL-1β, SOD, and CAT) were listed in Table 4. qPCR was performed in a 20 µl reaction mixture compris­ ing 2-uL cDNA sample, 0.4-µL each of forward and reverse primers (Table 2), 10-µL 2 × SYBR qPCR mix (Takara, Osaka, Japan). qPCR protocol involved the following steps: 94°C for 3 min, followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 94°C for 10 s and annealing for 30 s. The level of target gene mRNA expression was standardized with the mRNA expression level of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydroge­ nase (GAPDH) (Kim et al., 2020). The ΔΔCT was adjusted against an average from the control group. All samples were run in triplicate, and the linear amount of the target gene expression to the calibrator was calculated by 2−ΔΔCT.

Statistical analysis Data related to each strain’s growth performance and gene expression analysis were analyzed by SPSS version 20.0 (SPSS, IL, USA). The study was carried out with a 2 × 2 factorial design arrangement comprising the two breeds (NYC and DYC) and two treatments (control = 28±1°C; and HS = 35±1°C). Data were presented in the form of mean ± SEM. Meat quality data were subjected to a twoway ANOVA with treatments and breeds. Duncan’s mul­ tiple range test was conducted for significant interaction. Unpaired Student’s t-test was carried out to calculate the SEM and P-value of data related gene expression. P<0.05 was considered with statistical significance.

## Results

The impact of HS on meat color parameters varies among chicken strains

The impact of HS on the color parameters of raw chicken breast and thigh muscles was evaluated (Ta­ ble 3). The pH values of the muscle meat did not show significant differences between the HS and control (CN) groups in both NYC and DYC strains (P>0.05). However, HS treatment for 7 days signifi­ cantly increased the lightness (L*-value) (P<0.01) and decreased the redness (a*-value) (P<0.01) of breast muscle, while it did not significantly affect the yellowness (b*-value) (P>0.05). In thigh muscles, HS caused a significant reduction in redness (a*-value) (P<0.01) and an increase in yellowness (b*-value) (P<0.01) between different treatments and strain in­ teractions. Moreover, there was a significant increase in the lightness (L*-value) of thigh muscle between treatments in both NYC and DYC strains (P>0.05). These findings indicate that HS severely influenced the color of breast and thigh muscles, with more pro­ nounced effects observed in NYC.

Water loss, drip loss, cooking loss, and tenderness in breast and thigh muscles

The effects of HS on various parameters related to meat quality were assessed in the breast and thigh muscles (Table 4). In the breast muscles, HS signifi­ cantly increased the drip loss (P<0.05), cooking loss (P<0.05), and shear force (P<0.01) compared to the CN group. However, no significant differences were observed in water loss (P>0.05). In the thigh muscles, there were no significant differences in drip loss, cook­ ing loss, and water loss between the strains, treatments, or their interactions (P>0.05). The only significant change observed was in shear force, which increased in the HS group (P<0.05). These findings suggest that

HS can affect the meat quality of both breast and thigh muscles.

Histopathological changes in the spleen after 7 days of HS

Histopathological examination was conducted to as­ sess the impact of HS on the spleen, an important immune organ (Figure 1, a1, b1). Spleen tissues from the control groups of both NYC and DYC strains exhibited normal histological features, including white pulp (WP), red pulp (RP), and central arteriole (CA). However, various abnormal changes were observed in the splenic tissues of the HS groups, ranging from mild to moderate (Fig­ ure 1, a2–b4). In NYC, HS caused lymphoid depletion, infiltration of inflammatory cells, mild necrosis, fibrosis, and mild vacuolar degeneration. In DYC, HS resulted in moderate degeneration of WP and RP, mild vacuolar degeneration, necrosis, and infiltration of inflammatory cells. Both groups exhibited mild to moderate vacuole degeneration. In NYC, moderate to high red blood cell (RBC) hyperplasia was observed, whereas only mild hyperplasia was noted in DYC. Additionally, mild to moderate degeneration of the white pulp was observed in NYC, while DYC did not display this degeneration. Furthermore, mild to moderate degeneration of the red pulp was observed in NYC, contrasting with the absence of such degeneration in DYC.

HS modulated the mRNA expression levels of genes related to immune response

To investigate the influence of HS on immune re­ sponse, the expression levels of immune-related genes in spleen tissues were analyzed (Figure 2). The mRNA ex­ pression levels of interleukin-4 (IL-4) and IL-6 were sig­ nificantly upregulated in the HS group of NYC (P<0.05), while no significant differences were observed in DYC (P>0.05). However, there were no significant differences in the expression of IL-10 and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) be­

HS triggered oxidative stress in chicken The effect of HS on the antioxidant capacity of the chickens was examined by assessing the mRNA expres­ sion levels of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT) in liver and breast tissues (Figure 3). After 7 days of HS, the expression of CAT in the liver and breast tis­ sues was significantly lower in the HS group of NYC compared to the control group (P<0.05). However, no significant changes in CAT expression were observed be­ tween the HS and control groups of DYC (P>0.05). HS in both NYC and DYC strains (P>0.05) did not significantly

affect the expression levels of SOD in the breast and liver tissues. These results indicate that a 7-day thermal chal­ lenge induced oxidative stress in the HS group of NYC, as evidenced by disrupted balance between oxidants and antioxidant enzymes.

Overall, the results demonstrate that HS affects meat color, quality, immune response, and antioxidant capac­ ity in broiler chickens. The findings suggest that nor­ mal-sized chickens (NYC) are more susceptible to the negative effects of HS compared to dwarf-sized chick­ ens (DYC), indicating potential advantages of the dwarf strain under high ambient temperatures. Understanding these differential responses can provide valuable insights for developing strategies to mitigate the impact of heat stress on poultry production and improve the overall health and well-being of broiler chickens.

## Discussion

Previous studies have consistently shown that high ambient temperature has a major impact on all aspects of meat quality, primarily by inducing oxidative stress in skeletal muscle tissues. Specifically, heat stress (HS) has been found to lead to noticeable changes in meat color, characterized by increased lightness (L*), decreased redness (a*), and enhanced yellowness (b*) (Leishman et al., 2021). In our study, 7 days of HS has increased lightness (L*-value) and yellowness (b*-value), while reduced redness (a*-value) in NYC, which was consist­ ent with previous reports (Xing et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2017). This change in meat color might be due to high drip loss, which could result in a loss of red pigment (myoglobin) in the meat, causing a lighter (L*-value) and less red (a*-value) color in chicken meat (Malila et al., 2021). In the present study, the L* value was increased, and the b* value was reduced in the HS group of NYC, which means that HS increased lightness and reduced redness of meat in both breast and thigh muscle samples of NYC, which was consistent with results reported in recent studies (Küçüközet and Uslu, 2018; Malila et al., 2021). On the other hand, no signifi­ cant difference was noted in the meat color of DYC in both breast and thigh muscle tissues. These results might indicate that DYC has better thermoregulation than NYC, which was consistent with previous research re­

sults (Deeb and Cahaner, 2001 a; Hadad et al., 2014; Ndri et al., 2007). After 7 days of HS, no significant difference was observed in pH and water loss of breast and thigh muscle in both chicken strains. However, we found that heat stress increased shear force, drip loss, and cook loss significantly in NYC, which was in complete agreement with Hashizawa et al. (2013), who observed that chronic heat stress greatly affected the shearing force of breast muscle in broiler chicken. Another study conducted by Lu et al. (2007) has found that heat exposure for longer period of time significantly increased the lightness and drip loss in meat.

Moreover, the study investigated the mRNA expres­ sion of genes encoding antioxidant (SOD and CAT) en­ zymes. Results have shown that along with rise in ambient temperature, the hepatic and pectoral mRNA expression level of CAT antioxidant enzyme has reduced signifi­ cantly in NYC, which was consistent with the findings of Zeng et al. (2014), who found that chronic heat stress reduced CAT and SOD activities in serum of the broiler chicken. Another study on rats found that chronic stress significantly reduced the T-AOC (total antioxidant capac­ ity), SOD, and catalase activity in the brain (Pejić et al., 2016). The reduction in hepatic expression of CAT might be due to exhaustion of the antioxidant system after longterm exposure to heat stress. Heat stress might induce the lipid peroxidation process that led to the exhaustion of the antioxidant defense mechanism in broiler birds (Azad

et al., 2010). The present study also reported a signifi­ cant decline in the expression level of CAT in heat stress group of NYC. Likewise, Xue et al. (2017) observed a significant exhaustion in serum antioxidant activity when commercial broiler birds were challenged with cy­ clic heat. Under high ambient temperature, the exhaustion of the anti-oxidative enzymes in broiler chickens might be due to the increased production of ROS that triggered cellular injury (Roushdy et al., 2018). Likewise, another study reported that chronic heat stress reduced the gene expression levels of SOD and catalase enzymes in the heart tissues of broiler birds. Another study conducted on Pekin ducks by Zeng et al. (2014) testified that the SOD and catalase activity level was significantly diminished in hepatic tissues when Pekin ducks were exposed to acute heat stress. Similarly, a recent study has revealed that the negative impact of chronic heat stress on serum antioxi­ dant capacity as chronic heat stress reduced GSH, T-SOD activity, and T-AOC in broiler chicken (Ahmed-Farid et al., 2021). Our study did not observe any significant change in the expression level of SOD in both NYC and DYC while significant reduction was observed only in the CAT of NYC. The reduction in CAT gene expression level indicated that NYC was more vulnerable to oxida­ tive stress under hot environmental conditions.

Furthermore, any alteration in immune parameters such as cytokines were also considered as an indicator of cellular stress and important biomarkers of immunity. In this study, HS upregulated the splenic mRNA expres­ sion of IL-4 in the HS group of NYC, which was consist­ ent with a previous study (Saleh and Al-Zghoul, 2019) that indicated the development of the humoral responses under heat stress conditions. HS enhanced the expres­ sion level of IL-6 in NYC only, while IL-10 and IL-1β did not change significantly in any of the two chicken strains. These findings agreed with previous studies, which observed the expression level of pro-inflammatory cytokines was significantly upregulated under heat stress. It might be via activating immune functioning through increased proliferation of lymphocytes and macrophages under heat stress (He et al., 2019; Varasteh et al., 2015). Augmented expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and its increased proliferation may further result in tis­ sue damage. Thermal stress for a more extended period can cause a poor growth rate and a suppressed immune system in the animals (Jin et al., 2011). Nevertheless, in various stress conditions, pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines are released from different immune cells that impart a fundamental role in determining the immune status of living organisms (Bamias et al., 2014). Usually, pro-inflammatory cytokines could inflict inflammatory injury, while on other hand, anti-inflammatory cytokines may ameliorate inflammation and promote the healing process (Iyer and Cheng, 2012). These findings were aligned with the observations from the study conduct­ ed by Malila et al. (2021), which found that HS effects were not significant in the slow-growing chicken strain as compared to fast-growing local Thai native chicken.

Moreover, during the experiment, it was also observed that DYC chickens were comfortable even in harsh en­ vironmental conditions compared to NYC, which was consistent with the previous studies (Deeb and Cahaner, 2001 b; Sharifi et al., 2010; Yunis and Cahaner, 1999). One of the apparent reasons for this might be a small size and low growth rates of DYC birds compared to NYC (Hadad et al., 2014; Ndri et al., 2007).

Conclusions This study concludes that chickens with higher body weight and body size, represented by the normal yel­ low chicken (NYC) strain, were more vulnerable to the harmful effects of heat stress (HS). The research found that whereas DYC exhibited only modest changes in meat quality under high ambient temperature, HS dra­ matically reduced the quality of meat in NYC. Addi­ tionally, HS significantly affected the levels of gene expression in NYC that are involved in immunity and oxidative stress, which furthered the decline in meat quality. The meat quality was better and the immuno­ logical status was more resilient in DYC under HS cir­ cumstances. Nevertheless, further extensive research is needed to fully elucidate the underlying mechanisms of heat tolerance in dwarf chickens. These results pro­ vide valuable insights into the differential responses of chicken strains to HS and highlight the potential advan­ tages of dwarf-sized chickens in mitigating the nega­ tive effects of heat stress on meat quality and immune function.
